source: CK-12 Language Arts Grade 8 Concepts, Section 6.1, CC-BY-NC
notes: Class B document (13 units). Third language arts document. Covers claim/evidence/reasoning structure and counterargument. One ECU for the worked example analysis.

units.label: Title: Persuasive Writing: Building an Argument
Hook: a debate clip (video)
units.content_summary: Short video clip of two students debating whether school should start later, showing one making a much more convincing case than the other. Prompts: what made one argument stronger?

units.label: Learning Objectives (text)
units.content_summary: Objectives: state a clear claim; support a claim with evidence and reasoning; address a counterargument; structure a persuasive paragraph.

units.label: Claim: the foundation (text)
units.content_summary: A claim is the main argument or position you are defending — a debatable statement, not a fact. Example: 'School should start at 9am instead of 7:30am.' A strong claim is specific and arguable.

units.label: Evidence: supporting the claim (text)
units.content_summary: Evidence is factual support: statistics, expert quotes, research findings, or documented examples. Strong evidence comes from credible, relevant sources — not personal opinion alone.

units.label: Reasoning: connecting evidence to claim (text)
units.content_summary: Reasoning explains HOW the evidence supports the claim — it's the logical bridge. Evidence alone doesn't persuade; the writer must explain why that evidence matters for the argument.

units.label: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Three-block diagram showing Claim → Evidence → Reasoning as connected building blocks, with arrows showing how each supports the next, forming a complete argument.

units.label: Counterargument and rebuttal (text)
units.content_summary: A strong persuasive piece acknowledges the opposing view (counterargument) and then explains why the writer's position is still stronger (rebuttal). This shows the writer has considered multiple sides, building credibility.

units.label: Worked example: school start times (text)
units.content_summary: Full annotated paragraph: Claim (school should start later) + Evidence (CDC study: teens need 8-10 hours sleep, early start times cause chronic sleep deprivation) + Reasoning (later start aligns school with teen sleep biology) + Counterargument (parents' work schedules) + Rebuttal (staggered bus schedules could address this).

units.label: Worked example annotated diagram (image)
units.content_summary: The worked example paragraph shown with colour-coded highlighting: claim in blue, evidence in green, reasoning in yellow, counterargument/rebuttal in orange, matching the CER diagram structure.

units.label: Common weaknesses to avoid (text)
units.content_summary: Common mistakes: claim too vague or factual (not debatable); evidence from unreliable sources; missing reasoning (evidence just 'dropped in' without explanation); ignoring the counterargument entirely.

units.label: Practice: write your own argument (text)
units.content_summary: Writing task: choose one of three provided topics and write a persuasive paragraph including claim, evidence, reasoning, and at least one counterargument with rebuttal.
